extracted.intended_audience: law students, IP practitioners, policy advocates, NGO activists and industry observers interested in Indian pharmaceutical patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory commentary and policy analysis of Section 3(d) of the Indian Patents Act, focused on how the clause limits patenting of new forms/uses of known substances (particularly pharmaceuticals) and its interaction with TRIPS/Doha and case law. Useful for readers evaluating patentability, opposition strategies, or public-health policy impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(d) exclusions (text)
rubrics_metrics.description: "(d) the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in increased efficacy of that substance or the mere discovery of any new property or new use for a known substance or of the mere use of a known process, machine or apparatus unless such process results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary statutory exclusion: mere discoveries, new uses/properties of known substances, and mere use of known processes are not inventions unless they meet the further efficacy/new-product/new-reactant conditions. The article frames this text as the baseline 'test' that any pharmaceutical seeking a patent in India must clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of being a mere discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Because 'discovery' is not defined in the Act, it is interpreted via ordinary meaning and legislative history: discovery = finding out the use of a thing already known or finding a new way to do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance from dictionaries and legislative history: natural biological sequences found in nature are 'discoveries' (not patentable), while artificially engineered proteins representing new products (not normally found in nature) can be 'inventions' (patentable). The article uses this distinction to assess whether subject-matter is excluded as mere discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of being a new form of a known substance
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'new form of a known substance' is prima facie excluded unless it differs significantly in properties with regard to efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Explanation to Section 3(d) attempts to define the breadth of 'new form' (see separate entry listing derivatives). The article notes this definition can be very broad and may capture many derivatives unless they show significant efficacy differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for increased efficacy (substantial improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: New forms of known substances are patentable only when they 'differ significantly in properties with regard to efficacy' — not a trivial increment, but a substantial increase in efficacy over the known substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 3(d) is intended to prevent evergreening. Evaluators should look for meaningful, demonstrable efficacy improvements, not marginal or cosmetic changes. Case examples (e.g., court findings regarding Erlotinib) show courts assess whether the derivative crosses the efficacy threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation: derivatives considered the same substance (enumeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: "For the purposes of this clause, salts, esters, ethers, polymorphs, metabolites, pure form, particle size, isomers, mixtures of isomers, complexes, combinations and other derivatives of known substance shall be considered to be the same substance, unless they differ significantly in properties with regard to efficacy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumeration provides concrete classes likely treated as the 'same substance' — evaluators should treat such forms as part of the prior art unless evidence shows they significantly change efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process patentability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The mere use of a known process, machine or apparatus' is not patentable 'unless such process results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For process claims, merely using an existing machine/process is insufficient; the process must yield a new product or involve at least one new reactant to be considered inventive under Section 3(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability standards under TRIPS (Article 27)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 27 of TRIPS: patents shall be available for inventions 'provided that they are new, involve an inventive step and are capable of industrial application.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TRIPS sets minimum standards but leaves terms undefined; member states (including India) have discretion to interpret and refine novelty, inventive step, and utility/industrial applicability to suit national policy (e.g., tighter standards to prevent evergreening). The article argues Section 3(d) is a permissible refinement under TRIPS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doha Declaration public-health flexibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Doha Declaration: TRIPS 'does not and should not prevent Members from taking measures to protect public health' and reaffirms members' rights to grant compulsory licenses, define public emergencies, and determine exhaustion regimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These international statements provide legal/policy support for India's approach to limiting certain patents to protect access to medicines; they are relevant when assessing TRIPS-compatibility of national rules like Section 3(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-grant opposition and common grounds for opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the public, generic companies and NGOs can file pre-grant oppositions on grounds such as lack of novelty/anticipation, lack of significantly enhanced efficacy under Section 3(d), obviousness, and wrongful priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-grant opposition is a procedural tool often used in India to challenge weak pharma patents; the article cites Novartis and notes many oppositions have targeted antiretrovirals and cancer drugs. Patent applicants should anticipate such scrutiny and demonstrable evidence of enhanced efficacy if relying on derivatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction of 'new use' and 'new substance' under the Explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: A new use/indication for a derivative/new form can, under the Explanation, qualify the derivative as a 'new substance' if it 'differs significantly in properties with regard to efficacy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: obtaining a patent by claiming a novel therapeutic indication may fail if the new use does not amount to a significant efficacy difference; conversely, a genuinely new indication that demonstrates increased efficacy may treat the compound as a new substance and be patentable (illustrated by discussion of Erlotinib vs Gefitinib).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evergreening prevention principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3(d) aims to prevent 'evergreening'—the practice of patenting minor modifications of known drugs to extend monopoly periods without real therapeutic advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy evaluators should treat Section 3(d) as deliberately tightening patentability criteria to force focus on substantive innovation; patent offices and courts will scrutinize incremental changes and require evidence of real therapeutic benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy balancing criterion: access to medicines vs R&D incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: A core evaluative criterion in the debate: whether law should prioritize affordable access to medicines (public health) or stronger patent protection to incentivize pharmaceutical R&D and investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames choices and suggests possible middle-ground policy options (e.g., selective protection for life-saving drugs vs others), highlights consequences for investment and outsourcing, and notes international pressure and diplomatic mechanisms (trade sanctions, TRIPS-plus demands).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical evidentiary expectation for efficacy claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting that a derivative 'differs significantly in properties with regard to efficacy', applicants and courts expect substantive evidence of efficacy improvement rather than speculative or marginal data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article's case discussions imply that empirical clinical/experimental data comparing the derivative to prior art will be decisive; weak or purely theoretical claims of improved efficacy are unlikely to pass Section 3(d) scrutiny.
